name: Type 1 Diabetes
overview: Type 1 diabetes happens when the immune system mistakenly destroys the cells in the pancreas that make insulin — the hormone that moves sugar from the blood into the body's cells. Without insulin, blood sugar climbs to dangerous levels, so people with type 1 take insulin every day for life. It often starts in childhood but can appear at any age. With modern insulins, pumps, and glucose monitors, people with type 1 live full, active lives.

drugs.name: Rapid-acting insulin (Humalog, NovoLog)
drugs.note: Taken with meals to handle blood-sugar rises from food.

drugs.name: Long-acting insulin (Lantus, Tresiba)
drugs.note: Provides a steady background level of insulin all day.

drugs.name: Insulin pump with glucose monitor
drugs.note: Many people use these instead of multiple daily shots.

drugs.name: Glucagon (Baqsimi, Gvoke)
drugs.note: Raises blood sugar fast during a severe low.

redFlags: Vomiting, deep rapid breathing, fruity-smelling breath, or confusion can signal diabetic ketoacidosis — call 911 or go to the ER.

name: Prediabetes
overview: Prediabetes means your blood sugar is higher than normal but not yet high enough to count as type 2 diabetes. It's remarkably common — more than 1 in 3 American adults have it, and most don't know. The encouraging news: prediabetes is often reversible. Losing a modest amount of weight, moving more, and eating better can bring blood sugar back to normal and cut your risk of developing diabetes roughly in half.
symptoms: Usually no symptoms — most people don't know they have it
Darkened, velvety skin patches on the neck or armpits
Often found only through a routine blood test

drugs.name: Lifestyle changes
drugs.note: Losing 5-7% of body weight and walking regularly can cut diabetes risk about in half.

drugs.name: Metformin
drugs.note: Sometimes prescribed when lifestyle changes alone aren't enough.

drugs.name: Diabetes Prevention Program
drugs.note: A CDC-backed group program proven to lower the risk of type 2 diabetes.

redFlags: Extreme thirst, constant urination, blurry vision, or unplanned weight loss can mean diabetes has developed — seek same-day care.

name: Hyperthyroidism (Overactive Thyroid)
aka: Overactive thyroid, Graves' disease (most common cause)
overview: Hyperthyroidism means the thyroid gland in your neck makes too much thyroid hormone, putting your whole body into overdrive — heart racing, weight dropping, hands shaky, mind anxious. The most common cause is Graves' disease, where the immune system overstimulates the thyroid. It's very treatable: medicines can slow hormone production, and radioactive iodine or surgery offer lasting fixes. Most people feel like themselves again once hormone levels are back to normal.
symptoms: Weight loss despite a good appetite
Sweating more and feeling too warm
Bulging or irritated eyes (with Graves' disease)

drugs.name: Methimazole (Tapazole)
drugs.note: First-choice pill that slows the thyroid's hormone production.

drugs.name: Propranolol / Atenolol
drugs.note: Calms a racing heart and tremors while other treatment takes effect.

drugs.name: Radioactive iodine
drugs.note: A one-time capsule that shrinks overactive thyroid tissue.

drugs.name: Propylthiouracil (PTU)
drugs.note: An alternative used in early pregnancy or when methimazole isn't tolerated.

redFlags: Fever, a very fast heartbeat, and confusion or agitation can signal thyroid storm, a rare emergency — call 911 or go to the ER.

name: Low Testosterone
prevalence: About 2 in 100 men (more common with age)
overview: Testosterone naturally declines as men get older, but when levels drop well below normal, it can sap energy, mood, sex drive, and muscle strength. A simple morning blood test confirms the diagnosis — symptoms alone aren't enough, since fatigue and low libido have many causes, including poor sleep, stress, and depression. When true low T is found, testosterone replacement can help many men feel better, though it requires ongoing monitoring by a doctor.
symptoms: Loss of muscle and increased body fat

drugs.name: Testosterone gel (AndroGel)
drugs.note: A daily gel rubbed into the skin — one of the most common forms.

drugs.name: Testosterone injection (Depo-Testosterone)
drugs.note: A shot given every one to two weeks.

drugs.name: Testosterone patch (Androderm)
drugs.note: Worn on the skin and changed daily.

drugs.name: Lifestyle changes
drugs.note: Weight loss, exercise, and better sleep can raise levels naturally.

redFlags: If you're on testosterone therapy and develop chest pain, sudden shortness of breath, or a swollen painful leg, call 911 — these can signal a blood clot.

name: Metabolic Syndrome
overview: Metabolic syndrome isn't one disease — it's a cluster of risk factors that tend to show up together: a large waistline, high blood pressure, high blood sugar, high triglycerides, and low "good" cholesterol. Having three or more raises your risk of heart disease, stroke, and type 2 diabetes. About 1 in 3 American adults has it. The hopeful part: the same lifestyle changes — losing weight, exercising, eating better — improve all five at once.
symptoms: Usually no obvious symptoms day to day
High blood sugar on lab tests
High triglycerides or low "good" HDL cholesterol

drugs.name: Lifestyle changes
drugs.note: Weight loss, exercise, and healthier eating improve every part of the syndrome.

drugs.name: Atorvastatin (Lipitor)
drugs.note: Lowers cholesterol to protect the heart.

drugs.name: Lisinopril
drugs.note: A common choice for bringing blood pressure down.

drugs.name: Metformin
drugs.note: Helps control blood sugar when it starts creeping up.

redFlags: Chest pain, sudden weakness on one side, face drooping, or trouble speaking can signal a heart attack or stroke — call 911 right away.
